passage:
Week one: Lavanya wanted a book set that cost more than her monthly pocket money. She drew a jar on paper and coloured a bit each time she saved. Her sister Neelam laughed. "You'll give up."
Week two: At the stationery shop, glittery gel pens called to her. She picked them up, then looked at her paper jar and put them back.
Week five: The jar was full. Lavanya bought the book set. That night she told Neelam, "The pens would've been nice. But this is what I really wanted."

qa.q: What did Lavanya draw to track her saving?
qa.a: She drew a jar on paper and coloured a bit each time she saved.

qa.q: What might Lavanya have felt when she put the gel pens back?
qa.a: She may have felt a pull of disappointment but also determination to reach her goal.

qa.q: What helped Lavanya resist the impulse buy?
qa.a: Looking at her paper jar reminded her of the book set she really wanted.

qa.q: How might Neelam see Lavanya after week five?
qa.a: She may be surprised and respect her sister for sticking to her plan.

grounding: It shows a child saving toward a goal and resisting an impulse want over weeks.

passage: "Vishal, when I was twelve, I wanted real football boots. My father said, 'Save for them.' Every week I kept a little of my pocket money in a tin. Then the town fair came, with rides and sweets. My friends spent everything. I spent half my tin on one evening. The next morning I felt terrible. It took me two more months to get back to where I was. When I finally bought those boots, I wore them until they fell apart." Thomas Dadu laughed. "So, what's in your tin, and what's it for?"

qa.q: What did Thomas keep his savings in?
qa.a: He kept them in a tin.

qa.q: What does Thomas feeling terrible the next morning show?
qa.a: It shows he regretted spending on an impulse and losing progress toward his goal.

qa.q: What could Vishal learn from Thomas's story?
qa.a: That impulse spending can set back a real goal, so it helps to decide what you're saving for.

qa.q: How might Thomas's friends have seen his boots later?
qa.a: They may have admired them, knowing he saved for a long time.

grounding: An elder tells a story about saving toward a goal and the cost of an impulse want.

passage: The school fair had begun, and Yusuf had just enough pocket money for one thing. His geometry box had broken that week, and the maths test was on Monday. But the slime stall was glowing green and purple, and his friends were already squishing it. His sister Preeti tugged his sleeve. "What do you need?" Yusuf sighed. "The geometry box." "And what do you want?" "Slime." He stood between the stalls for a long moment. Then he bought the geometry box. Preeti let him hold her slime for five minutes.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf need a new geometry box?
qa.a: His geometry box had broken that week, and the maths test was on Monday.

qa.q: What does Yusuf standing between the stalls for a long moment suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt torn between what he needed and what he wanted.

qa.q: How did Preeti help Yusuf decide?
qa.a: She asked him to separate what he needed from what he wanted.

qa.q: How might Preeti see Yusuf's choice at the fair?
qa.a: She probably sees that giving up the slime was hard for him, which may be why she let him hold hers for five minutes.

grounding: It shows a child deciding between a need and an impulse want with limited pocket money.

passage: Sahil kept his pocket money in an old steel tiffin box under his bed in their Chennai flat. The goal was written on a sticky note on the lid: 'Cricket bat, ₹900.' After four months he had ₹640. On Saturday, at the Pondy Bazaar pavement stalls with his sister Dolma, he saw a yo-yo that lit up blue and green. ₹150. 'Ooh,' he breathed. 'Need or want?' Dolma asked, grinning. 'Want. Really, really want.' He turned it over in his hand. It would be fun for a day or two. The bat would be for the whole season. He put it back. On the way home, he did buy new chappals, because his old ones had snapped. That was a need.

qa.q: How much money had Sahil saved after four months?
qa.a: He had saved ₹640.

qa.q: How was Sahil feeling as he turned the yo-yo over in his hand?
qa.a: He felt torn, weighing a day or two of fun against the bat he wanted for the whole season.

qa.q: What helped Sahil stick to his savings goal?
qa.a: Having the goal written on the lid, and pausing to ask whether the yo-yo was a need or a want.

qa.q: How might Dolma see her brother's choice?
qa.a: She might be impressed that he walked away from something he really wanted, all by himself.

grounding: Shows a child saving toward a goal and choosing between a need and an impulse want.

passage: 'Dadu, look! Two hundred rupees from Mashi for my birthday!' Jeevan dadu lowered his newspaper. 'Very rich man now. Plans?' 'Stickers! The shiny football ones. A whole pack is two hundred.' 'Hmm. And your pencil box?' Anirban looked at it. The lid hung by one hinge. 'It still works. Sort of.' 'Sort of.' Dadu smiled. 'What did you say you wanted most last month?' 'A proper football. But that's so much money.' 'What if some goes in this jar every time?' Dadu tapped an empty pickle jar. Anirban chewed his lip. 'Hundred in the jar, fifty for a pencil box, fifty for stickers?' 'Your money, your choice.' 'Deal. I'm writing FOOTBALL on the jar.'

qa.q: How much birthday money did Anirban get from Mashi?
qa.a: He got two hundred rupees.

qa.q: What does Anirban chewing his lip suggest?
qa.a: He was torn between wanting stickers now and saving for the football he wanted most, and was working out a plan.

qa.q: Why did Dadu's approach help Anirban decide?
qa.a: He asked questions and suggested a jar but left the final choice to Anirban, so the plan felt like his own.

qa.q: What would change if Dadu had taken the money away to save for him?
qa.a: Anirban might have felt cheated and wouldn't have practised deciding between needs, wants and a saving goal.

grounding: Shows a child dividing money between a need, a want and a saving goal.

passage:
When I was eleven I got twenty rupees pocket money every week. I spent it on chips and cola with my friend Jasleen after school.
I'm Tanuja. Then I saw a cricket bat in the sports shop. It cost a lot more than I had.
I made a chart on my wall, with a box for each week. Every time I skipped the snacks, I coloured a box. Some weeks I gave in and bought chips. Jasleen teased me.
After four months, I had enough. I bought the bat myself.
When I hit my first six with it, I felt richer than any packet of chips.

qa.q: What did Tanuja see in the sports shop?
qa.a: A cricket bat.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel on hitting the first six with the new bat?
qa.a: Tanuja felt proud and happy, richer than any packet of chips.

qa.q: What helped Tanuja reach the goal?
qa.a: A chart to track each week, and choosing the bat over snacks most weeks.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel after seeing the bat?
qa.a: Jasleen may feel impressed, even after teasing Tanuja.

grounding: A student saves pocket money toward a goal, choosing it over impulse snacks.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 6 school fair activity. Sudha Iyer.
Each child had fifty paper rupees to spend at the class market. The task: buy a notebook, a pencil, and one fun thing.
Kiran (eleven) went straight to the toy stall and spent forty on a spinning top. Then he had only ten left, not enough for the notebook.
He looked upset. “I didn't think.”
We talked about needs and wants. He traded the top back for the notebook, pencil and a small eraser.
He said, “Next time I'll buy the needs first.”
Next step: I'll repeat the activity next term.

qa.q: How much did Kiran spend on the spinning top?
qa.a: He spent forty on a spinning top.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel when he couldn't buy the notebook?
qa.a: He felt upset and frustrated with himself.

qa.q: What did Kiran learn from the activity?
qa.a: To buy needs first before spending on wants.

qa.q: How might the teacher feel when Kiran says he'll buy needs first?
qa.a: The teacher would likely feel pleased that he learned from his mistake.

grounding: A teacher records an eleven-year-old learning to prioritise needs over wants.

passage:
Monday
I'm saving for a football. I have half the money in my tin.
Today at the stationery shop there was a shiny keychain with a light in it. I really wanted it. Vishal said, “Just buy it. It's small.”
I held it for a long time. Then I thought, if I buy this, the football takes longer.
I put it back. Vishal said I was boring.
When I got home I counted my tin again. Still half. But half is closer than less than half.
I'm going to play football with the old ball tomorrow. — Harish

qa.q: What did Harish see at the stationery shop?
qa.a: A shiny keychain with a light in it.

qa.q: How did Harish feel while holding the keychain?
qa.a: Harish felt tempted and torn between the keychain and the football.

qa.q: What choice did Harish make, and why does it make sense?
qa.a: Harish put the keychain back to keep saving for the football, which was the bigger goal.

qa.q: How does Vishal see Harish's choice?
qa.a: Vishal thinks Harish is boring for not buying the keychain.

grounding: A student resists an impulse buy to keep saving toward a goal.

passage:
In the small town, Vinita kept her pocket money in a clay piggy bank. She was saving for new school shoes; her old ones had a hole.
At the Sunday fair, her sister Uma pointed at a glittery plastic tiara. "That's so pretty!"
Vinita wanted it badly. She had enough coins in her pocket.
She held the tiara. Then she thought of her wet sock last monsoon.
"Next time," she said, putting it down.
At home, she dropped her coins in the piggy bank. It was getting heavy. Uma rolled her eyes. "Boring." But Vinita smiled.

qa.q: What was Vinita saving for?
qa.a: New school shoes.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling when she held the tiara?
qa.a: Vinita felt tempted and torn between the pretty tiara and her shoes.

qa.q: What helped Vinita decide, and what could she try next time?
qa.a: Remembering her wet sock reminded her the shoes were a real need; next time she could ask a trusted adult to help her plan for both.

qa.q: How does Uma see Vinita's choice?
qa.a: Uma thinks it's boring, since she was excited about the tiara.

grounding: A child in a small town chooses her saving goal over an impulse purchase at a fair.

passage:
In Accra, Kofi was saving for football boots. His old ones pinched his toes.
After school, his friend Tomas bought a big bag of sweets and a toy car from the corner shop. "Get one too!"
Kofi looked at his coins. He loved those toy cars.
He counted in his head how many more weeks until he had enough for the boots. If he spent it now, it would be longer.
"I'll just have one of your sweets," he said.
Tomas laughed and shared. That weekend, Kofi's grandmother saw the jar and smiled. "You're nearly there."

qa.q: What was Kofi saving for?
qa.a: Football boots.

qa.q: What was Kofi feeling when he looked at his coins?
qa.a: Kofi felt tempted and torn, because he loved the toy cars but wanted the boots.

qa.q: What helped Kofi stick to his goal?
qa.a: Thinking about how spending now would delay the boots helped him choose, and a trusted adult like his grandmother can keep encouraging him.

qa.q: How might Tomas see Kofi's choice?
qa.a: Tomas doesn't seem to mind and happily shares, so it doesn't hurt their friendship.

grounding: A child in Ghana resists an impulse buy to keep saving for boots he needs.

passage:
At the school fete, each student had a small amount of pocket money to spend. Dhruv had to buy a geometry box he'd lost, and then could spend the rest.
The game stalls were loud and bright. Deepika tugged him toward the ring toss. "Win a giant teddy!"
Dhruv looked at his money, then at the stationery stall at the back.
"If I play first and lose, I won't have enough for the box."
"But the teddy!"
"The box is for exams." He bought it first. Then he played ring toss once with what was left, and missed.
He laughed anyway. "At least I've got a compass."

qa.q: What did Dhruv have to buy at the fete?
qa.a: A geometry box.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he looked at his money and then at the stationery stall?
qa.a: Dhruv felt torn between the fun stalls and what he needed.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do that helped him handle both a need and a want?
qa.a: He bought the needed box first, then used what was left for fun.

qa.q: How might Deepika see Dhruv's choice?
qa.a: Deepika might think he's too careful at first, but she sees he still had fun after buying the box.

grounding: At a school fete, a child buys what he needs before spending on a want.

passage:
I'm Parul. My cousin Tanuja stayed with us for the summer, saving her pocket money in a steel tin for a bicycle bell and basket. She had a list taped to the tin with the price, and she crossed off each amount she added.
At the Sunday fair near our lane, there was a stall of glitter slime in tiny jars. Tanuja stood there a long time. She opened her purse, closed it, opened it again. I didn't say anything. Honestly, I wanted to see what she'd do.
She bought a small bottle of water, because it was hot, and nothing else. On the walk back she was quiet. That night she added the rest to the tin and crossed off another line. She looked at the list for ages.

qa.q: What was Tanuja saving her pocket money for?
qa.a: She was saving for a bicycle bell and basket.

qa.q: What does Tanuja opening and closing her purse suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests she was tempted and torn between the slime and her goal.

qa.q: What would you advise a child who, like Tanuja, is tempted by something at a fair?
qa.a: Pause and ask whether it's a need or a want, and whether the goal matters more; talking it over with a trusted grown-up can help too.

qa.q: Why might Parul have stayed silent instead of giving advice?
qa.a: Parul was curious to see what Tanuja would choose, and staying quiet let the decision be Tanuja's own.

grounding: Illustrates, through an observer, a child choosing a need over an impulse want while saving toward a goal.

passage:
First day of Durga Puja. Anirban had been saving his pocket money since July for a proper football, the kind with stitched panels. He had most of it.
Fourth day, Ashtami. The pandal stalls were full of flashing toys and fried things. Kishore bought a light-up spinner and waved it in front of Anirban's face. "Come on, it's Puja." Anirban spent a little on phuchka, because he was really hungry after the long walk, and then walked away from the spinner stall twice.
Tenth day, after the immersion, the spinner had stopped lighting up. Kishore shook it and frowned.
A week later, Anirban carried his new football to the park. Kishore asked, "Can I play?"
"Obviously," said Anirban.

qa.q: What was Anirban saving his pocket money for?
qa.a: A proper football, the kind with stitched panels.

qa.q: Why did Anirban walk away from the spinner stall twice?
qa.a: Anirban felt tempted by the spinner but determined to reach his football goal, so he pulled himself away.

qa.q: Which choice at the pandal was reasonable, and why?
qa.a: Buying phuchka when he was really hungry was fine, because food then was a real need, unlike a toy he'd only wanted in the moment.

qa.q: How might Kishore see the broken spinner when Anirban arrives with the football?
qa.a: Kishore might feel a bit let down or envious, noticing the spinner didn't last while the football will.

grounding: Shows a child over Puja weeks separating a real need from impulse wants while saving for a goal.

passage:
Vishal, sit. You want those new shoes with lights? Let me tell you about my Dussehra, sixty years back.
I was maybe nine. All year I saved coins from errands in a tin under my cot, for a real cricket bat. Just before Dussehra I had enough. At the fair there was a tin toy gun that went click-click. I wanted it so badly my stomach hurt.
Then Amma said my school shoes had a hole, and there was no extra for new ones before the rains.
I stood between the toy stall and the cobbler for a long time. I bought the shoes. The bat came the next summer. The gun, I don't even remember why I wanted it. But I remember the bat. That's your Siddharth Dada's whole secret.

qa.q: Where did the young Siddharth keep his coins?
qa.a: Siddharth kept them in a tin under his cot.

qa.q: How did young Siddharth feel at the fair when he saw the toy gun?
qa.a: Young Siddharth wanted it so badly his stomach hurt; Siddharth felt strongly tempted.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Choosing the shoes over the toy gun mattered, because the shoes were a real need before the rains, while the gun was a passing want.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt when her son chose the shoes?
qa.a: Amma might have felt relieved and proud, since she couldn't pay for new shoes herself.

grounding: Illustrates an elder, Siddharth Dada, recalling how as a child Siddharth chose a real need over an impulse want and still reached his saving goal later.

passage:
Yamini, eleven, had been saving her pocket money since the monsoon for a new school bag; the zip on her old one had broken twice. It was nearly Diwali and she had almost enough.
Then, at the Diwali market, with her cousin Abhinav, she saw a glowing slime kit in a stall. Her hand went to her purse.
"Buy it!" said Abhinav. "It's Diwali!"
The crowd pushed, the stall owner said, "Last one!" and Yamini's heart thumped. She thought of the broken zip, the books falling out on the bus.
"Not today," she said, pulling her hand back.
Abhinav rolled his eyes. But two weeks later, when she walked into school with a new bag, he asked, "How did you save for that?"

qa.q: What did Yamini see at the stall?
qa.a: She saw a glowing slime kit.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when the stall owner said "Last one!"?
qa.a: Yamini felt tempted and pressured, her heart thumping, torn between the fun toy and the bag she needed.

qa.q: How could Yamini handle a moment like this next time?
qa.a: She could remember what she is saving for, as she did with the broken zip, and give herself time before buying rather than deciding in the rush.

qa.q: How does Abhinav's view change by the end?
qa.a: Abhinav first thinks she's being boring, but later is impressed and curious about how she saved for the bag.

grounding: Shows a child choosing a needed item she saved for over a tempting impulse buy during a festival rush.
